Jump proposes pantheism, unifying laws, and natural moral laws, then asserts equal or better explanation without adequate support; that is weak model comparison, not explicitly treating a claim as true because it remains unrefuted.
The move asks why a higher law yields life-supporting values, but within this move it does not explicitly exempt God from an equivalent explanatory demand or articulate a different standard.

McLatchie asks what explains a higher law's life-conducive form and applies an explanatory demand rather than exempting God within this move; the unanswered necessity possibility is a substantive limitation.
The exemption from a further cause is tied to the explicit contingent-versus-necessary distinction, a principled difference; the unsupported step is identifying God as the best necessary candidate.

McLatchie rejects a bare appeal to possible future explanations and asks for judgment from present evidence; he does not infer theism merely because a future natural account has not been proved.
McLatchie argues that bare future possibilities do not defeat a present best explanation; he still must establish that present superiority, but he does not treat non-disproof as proof.

Jump describes an eternal all-powerful nature and simply asserts equal scope, power, and priors; this lacks supporting model detail, but no premise covertly assumes the same equality conclusion in a circular structure.
